title: Knowledge Builds on Knowledge
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart takes stock of his literacy Foundations Framework and admits that one component, Build and Organize Knowledge, is unfinished. For the other components he sees a clear pattern, quantity before quality, plus three levers for noncognitive factors. For knowledge he offers one organizing insight, drawn from Hirsch and Willingham: knowledge builds on knowledge. He illustrates it with looking up word nuances, which only works because he already knows the word. He then gives world history and grammar examples, such as locating Anatolia before reading about the Hittites or knowing subjects and verbs before comma rules. The post argues that a profession eager for higher-order thinking has to accept that a robust knowledge base must come first.
points: Across argument, reading, writing, and speaking/listening, the pattern is that quantity precedes quality, so teachers should first increase volume and then improve it efficiently.
Stuart added knowledge to the Framework after seeing that it affects how well students read and argue.
The central claim, drawn from Hirsch and Willingham, is that knowledge builds on knowledge, so higher-order thinking depends on a robust base.
His dictionary example shows that you must already know a word to look it up and learn its nuances.
Classroom examples such as locating Anatolia before reading about the Hittites, or knowing subjects and verbs before commas, show prior knowledge multiplying what students learn.
quotes: For argument, reading, writing, and speaking/listening, a general pattern emerges: quantity precedes quality. From this, we have an obvious strategy: increase the amount of reading, writing, speaking, listening, and arguing that our students do, and then use efficient means for improving the quality of the reading, writing, and so on, that our students are capable of.

But the more I taught with the Framework in view, the more I led workshops on it, the more I researched its components, the more I came to see that knowledge is non-negotiable. For example, it affects how well we read and how well we argue.

So, while I don't have the exact “Next Steps” for knowledge-building like I do for the other parts of the Framework, I do have one thing to share: knowledge builds on knowledge. This insight, impressed upon me in reading E. D. Hirsch, Jr. and Daniel Willingham especially, is one of those “hiding right in front of us” things.

In a profession that wants to jump straight into the highest order thinking, we struggle with the notion that there needs to be a robust knowledge base before the highest order thoughts can come. Consider a simple example: whenever I write a blog post, it's common for me to wonder at the exact meaning of a word.

Had I not known the word I was searching for to begin with, I wouldn't have been able to look it up, and even if I had, I wouldn't have been able to learn the added nuances that my quick search garnered. Knowing the word enabled me to know more about the word. Without the knowledge, I wouldn't have gained the knowledge.

If a student doesn't know where Anatolia is, she won't gain as much knowledge from reading a selection on the Hittites as a student who can locate Anatolia. Or when teaching mechanics in English class (there's an amazing set of books for that), the rules for comma usage don't help all that much if you don't know what makes a sentence.
